name: Probability Theory and Statistics
description: A source-grounded path from probability models and random variables to estimation, confidence intervals, regression and responsible hypothesis testing, with original worked examples and practice.
limitations: Based on the supplied course archive, including older CSE1210 materials; this is not a statement of current examination rules.
Exercises are newly authored practice, not official past-exam questions or a prediction of exam coverage. Open exercises require self-review against the rubric and are ungraded.
Most lecture PDFs are image-based. Their supplied transcription was cross-checked against sampled rendered slides and the textbook; not every slide received visual review.
Normal approximations, distribution parameterizations, quantile conventions and independence assumptions are stated where used. N(mu, sigma^2) always uses variance as its second parameter.

Bootstrap and variance tests extend the main lecture sequence using the supplied book/course overview. No external Grasple tasks, recording videos or unavailable computer-assignment datasets are reproduced.

topics.name: Events, counting and probability models
topics.description: Build a sample space before applying probability rules.

skills.name: Construct probability models
skills.description: Check nonnegativity, normalization and event operations.

skills.name: Count equiprobable outcomes
skills.description: Distinguish ordered selections, subsets and replacement.

lesson.title: From experiment to event
paragraphs: A sample space lists possible elementary outcomes; an event is a subset of that space. For two die rolls, ordered pairs are elementary outcomes, whereas a sum is a function of those pairs. The sums 2 through 12 are not equally likely. State the random mechanism before counting favorable outcomes.

A probability law assigns nonnegative mass with total one. For disjoint events, probabilities add. In general P(A union B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A intersection B), and P(A complement)=1-P(A). If A is contained in B, P(A) cannot exceed P(B). These are quick consistency checks for a proposed model.

lesson.title: Counting with a reason
paragraphs: For three distinct ordered roles chosen from six people there are 6*5*4=120 assignments. For an unordered committee of three, divide by 3! to get 20. With replacement there are 6^3 ordered selections. Dividing a favorable count by the total is justified only when the elementary outcomes in those counts are equiprobable.

Worked example: two independent fair six-sided dice have 36 ordered outcomes. A sum of at least 11 occurs in (5,6), (6,5), (6,6), so its probability is 3/36=1/12. Treating the eleven possible sums as equally likely would give the wrong answer.

exercises.title: Ordered selections
exercises.prompt: Six distinct students fill chair, secretary and treasurer roles. Nobody holds two roles. How many assignments exist?
exercises.explanation: There are 6 choices, then 5, then 4: 6*5*4=120.

exercises.title: Unordered committee
exercises.prompt: How many committees of three can be chosen from eight distinct people? A committee has no internal roles.
exercises.explanation: Choose(8,3)=8*7*6/(3*2*1)=56; ordering a committee would overcount six times.

exercises.title: Union without double counting
exercises.prompt: P(A)=0.45, P(B)=0.35 and P(A intersection B)=0.15. Find P(A union B).
exercises.explanation: Subtract the overlap counted twice: 0.45+0.35-0.15=0.65.

exercises.title: A proposed probability law
exercises.prompt: On outcomes a,b,c, someone assigns masses 0.4, 0.7 and -0.1. The sum is one. Explain whether this is a probability law.
exercises.explanation: It is invalid because the mass of c is negative. Normalization alone is insufficient.
rubric: Identify the negative mass.
State both nonnegativity and total mass one as necessary conditions.

exercises.title: Two high dice
exercises.prompt: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled independently. What is the probability that their sum is at least 11?
exercises.explanation: Only (5,6), (6,5), (6,6) qualify among 36 equiprobable ordered pairs.

exercises.title: Sampling without replacement
exercises.prompt: A bag has four red and six blue tokens. Draw two uniformly without replacement. What is the probability both are red?
exercises.explanation: The sequential probability is (4/10)(3/9)=2/15; the second draw has changed composition.

exercises.title: Repeated outcomes allowed
exercises.prompt: A length-four code uses symbols 0,1,2,3,4. Repetition and a leading zero are allowed. How many codes exist?
exercises.explanation: Each position has five choices independently of the others: 5^4=625.

exercises.title: Disjoint versus independent
exercises.prompt: Events A and B are disjoint and each has probability 0.3. Can they be independent? Justify with the defining equation.
exercises.explanation: Their intersection has probability zero, but independence would require 0.3*0.3=0.09. Thus they are dependent.
rubric: Use disjointness to get intersection probability zero.
Compare with the positive product 0.09.

topics.name: Conditioning, Bayes and independence
topics.description: Update probabilities using information and partition a population correctly.

skills.name: Condition and reverse conditionals
skills.description: Use multiplication, total probability and Bayes with explicit denominators.

skills.name: Diagnose independence
skills.description: Separate marginal, conditional, pairwise and mutual independence.

lesson.title: Restrict the reference population
paragraphs: P(A given B)=P(A intersection B)/P(B) when P(B)>0. Conditioning changes the reference population. It does not reverse automatically: the proportion of faulty items that trigger an alarm is different from the proportion of alarms caused by faulty items.

If B1,...,Bk partition the space, P(A)=sum P(A given Bi)P(Bi). Bayes then gives P(Bj given A)=P(A given Bj)P(Bj)/P(A). Write numerator and denominator separately to avoid forgetting an alternative source of A.

lesson.title: Worked update and independence pitfalls
paragraphs: Suppose a component is faulty with probability 0.1, an alarm detects a fault with probability 0.8, and a sound component triggers an alarm with probability 0.2. The alarm probability is 0.8*0.1+0.2*0.9=0.26, so the posterior fault probability is 0.08/0.26=4/13. The false-alarm population can dominate despite a sensitive detector.

Independence means P(A intersection B)=P(A)P(B). Pairwise independence of three events checks three pairs, but mutual independence also requires the triple intersection equation. Conditioning on a shared outcome can destroy independence; never infer a conditional product from a marginal one without checking.

exercises.title: Alarm posterior
exercises.prompt: A fault has probability 0.1. An alarm occurs with probability 0.8 given a fault and 0.2 otherwise. Given an alarm, what is the fault probability?
exercises.explanation: P(fault and alarm)=0.08 and P(alarm)=0.08+0.18=0.26; divide to obtain 4/13.

exercises.title: A mixed production line
exercises.prompt: Factory A supplies 60% of parts with defect probability 0.02; B supplies 40% with defect probability 0.05. Find the probability a random supplied part is defective.
exercises.explanation: Weight each defect rate by its source probability: 0.6*0.02+0.4*0.05=0.032.

exercises.title: Independence check
exercises.prompt: P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5 and P(A intersection B)=0.2. Are A and B independent? Explain and calculate P(A given B).
exercises.explanation: The product 0.4*0.5 equals 0.2, so they are independent. P(A given B)=0.2/0.5=0.4.
rubric: Check intersection equals product.
Compute the conditional probability using the nonzero denominator.

exercises.title: Condition on a die restriction
exercises.prompt: A fair six-sided die shows an even value. What is the probability the value exceeds three?
exercises.explanation: The conditioned space is {2,4,6}; two of its three equally likely outcomes exceed three.

exercises.title: Two failures
exercises.prompt: Components fail independently with probabilities 0.2 and 0.3. What is the probability at least one fails?
exercises.explanation: The probability neither fails is 0.8*0.7=0.56; its complement is 0.44.

exercises.title: Pairwise is not mutual
exercises.prompt: Flip two independent fair coins. Let A mean the first is heads, B the second is heads, and C that both agree. Show that the three events are pairwise independent but not mutually independent.
exercises.explanation: Each event has probability 1/2; each pair intersects only at HH, probability 1/4. The triple also has probability 1/4, whereas the product of the three marginals is 1/8.
rubric: List or reason from HH, HT, TH, TT.
Check all three pair products.
Compare the triple intersection with 1/8.

exercises.title: Sequential update
exercises.prompt: A bag has two red and one blue token. Draw two uniformly without replacement. Given that the first token is red, what is the chance the second is red?
exercises.explanation: After the stated observation one red and one blue token remain.

exercises.title: Conditioning creates dependence
exercises.prompt: Two independent fair coins are flipped. Given that at least one is heads, are their heads events still independent? Calculate the relevant probabilities.
exercises.explanation: The remaining outcomes are HH, HT, TH. Each heads event has conditional probability 2/3, but their intersection has conditional probability 1/3, not 4/9.
rubric: Identify the three conditioned outcomes.
Compute marginals 2/3 and intersection 1/3.
Conclude conditional dependence.

topics.name: Distributions and exploratory summaries
topics.description: Connect pmfs, densities and cdfs to empirical data summaries.

skills.name: Use cdfs and densities
skills.description: Normalize distributions, integrate probabilities and invert cdfs.

skills.name: Summarize observed data
skills.description: Interpret ecdfs, density histograms, medians and quartiles.

lesson.title: Mass is not density
paragraphs: A discrete pmf assigns point probabilities whose sum is one. A continuous density integrates to one, but its height need not be at most one. Probabilities are areas: P(a<X<=b)=F(b)-F(a), with F(x)=P(X<=x). For continuous X every singleton has probability zero; for a discrete X the cdf jumps by the point mass.

For f(x)=2x on [0,1], integration gives F(x)=x^2 within the support, zero below and one above. The median solves F(m)=1/2, so m=1/sqrt(2). Finding a quantile means inverting cumulative probability, not taking a fraction of the support length unless the distribution is uniform.

lesson.title: Data are a sample, not the population law
paragraphs: The empirical cdf at x is the fraction of observations no greater than x. A density-normalized histogram uses height=count/(sample size * bin width); areas, not heights, represent relative frequency when bins have different widths. Boxplots emphasize median, quartiles and spread but do not uniquely identify a distribution.

For observations 1,2,2,7, the empirical cdf at 2 is 3/4, the mean is 3 and the median is 2. Quantile conventions vary in finite samples, so an exercise must specify interpolation or order-statistic rules. Outliers pull the mean strongly; the median is more resistant.

exercises.title: Normalize a density
exercises.prompt: Let f(x)=c*x for 0<=x<=2 and zero otherwise. What value of c makes it a density?
exercises.explanation: Integral_0^2 c*x dx=2c, so c=1/2.

exercises.title: Read a cdf jump
exercises.prompt: X has masses P(X=0)=0.2, P(X=2)=0.5, P(X=5)=0.3. Find F(2).
exercises.explanation: The cdf includes the mass at its argument: P(X<=2)=0.2+0.5.

exercises.title: Probability from area
exercises.prompt: X has density 2x on [0,1]. Find P(1/2<X<=1).

exercises.title: Empirical cdf
exercises.prompt: For data 1,2,2,7, what is the empirical cdf at x=2?
exercises.explanation: Three of four observations are <=2, including both ties.

exercises.title: Unequal histogram bins
exercises.prompt: A density histogram has 100 observations; 20 lie in a bin of width 2. What should the bin height be?
exercises.explanation: Height=20/(100*2)=0.1; multiplying by width gives relative frequency 0.2.

exercises.title: Median under a stated convention
exercises.prompt: Use the average of the middle two observations for an even sample. Find the median of 3,4,8,10,12,19.
exercises.explanation: The ordered middle values are 8 and 10, giving (8+10)/2=9.

exercises.title: A height above one
exercises.prompt: Is the function f(x)=4 on [0,1/4] and zero elsewhere a valid density? Explain why a density above one does or does not violate probability axioms.
exercises.explanation: It is nonnegative and integrates to 4*(1/4)=1. Density height is not a point probability; area determines probability.
rubric: Check the integral and nonnegativity.
Distinguish density from probability.

exercises.title: Quantile inversion
exercises.prompt: A continuous distribution has cdf F(x)=x^2 on [0,1]. Determine its 0.25 quantile.
exercises.explanation: Solve q^2=0.25 with q in [0,1], hence q=0.5.

topics.name: Choose and parameterize a distribution
topics.description: Match Bernoulli, binomial, geometric, Poisson, uniform, exponential, Pareto and normal models to mechanisms.

skills.name: Model counts and trials
skills.description: Check fixed-trial, independence and rate assumptions.

skills.name: Model continuous measurements
skills.description: Use rate, scale, support and normal standardization consistently.

lesson.title: Discrete mechanisms
paragraphs: A Bernoulli(p) variable is a success indicator. The sum of n independent Bernoulli(p) trials is Bin(n,p), with mass choose(n,k)p^k(1-p)^(n-k), mean np and variance np(1-p). A geometric variable here counts trials until the first success, starting at 1: P(X=k)=(1-p)^(k-1)p and E[X]=1/p.

A Poisson(lambda) variable counts events with mean and variance lambda. For a homogeneous Poisson process with rate r, the count in time t has parameter rt, assuming independent increments and a constant rate. Counts without replacement are not binomial in general; heterogeneous or dependent trials also invalidate the simple model.

lesson.title: Continuous mechanisms and units
paragraphs: Uniform(a,b) assigns probability by interval length. Exponential(lambda) uses a rate, has survival e^(-lambda*t), mean 1/lambda and the memoryless property. Pareto(xm,alpha) has survival (xm/x)^alpha for x>=xm; its mean exists only for alpha>1 and variance only for alpha>2. Such heavy tails matter when considering CLT assumptions.

For X~N(mu,sigma^2), standardize with Z=(X-mu)/sigma, using the standard deviation rather than variance. Example: X~N(10,4) gives P(X<=12)=Phi(1), approximately 0.8413. For an exponential rate 2 per hour, P(X>0.5 hours)=e^-1; converting time without converting rate changes the model.

exercises.title: Binomial event
exercises.prompt: Four independent trials each succeed with probability 1/2. What is the probability of exactly two successes?

exercises.title: Geometric waiting
exercises.prompt: Independent attempts succeed with probability 1/4. X counts attempts including the first success. What is E[X]?
exercises.explanation: For the trials-until-success convention, E[X]=1/p=4; failures before success would have mean 3.

exercises.title: Poisson time scaling
exercises.prompt: Events follow a homogeneous Poisson process at rate 3 per minute. What is the expected number in four minutes?
exercises.explanation: The interval count is Poisson(3*4), with expectation 12.

exercises.title: Exponential survival
exercises.prompt: X is exponential with rate 2 per hour. What is P(X>0.5 hours)?
exercises.explanation: The survival function is exp(-lambda*t), hence exp(-2*0.5).

exercises.title: Pareto tail
exercises.prompt: P(X>x)=(2/x)^3 for x>=2. What is P(X>4)?
exercises.explanation: Substitute x=4 into the given survival: (2/4)^3=1/8.

exercises.title: Normal variance convention
exercises.prompt: X~N(10,4), where 4 is the variance. Given Phi(1)=0.8413, find P(X<=12).

exercises.title: Memorylessness reasoning
exercises.prompt: A lifetime X is exponential with rate lambda>0. Derive P(X>s+t given X>s) for s,t>=0 and explain the interpretation.
exercises.explanation: The ratio e^(-lambda*(s+t))/e^(-lambda*s)=e^(-lambda*t). Having survived s does not change the model for remaining lifetime; this is a model property, not universal physical behavior.
rubric: Use the conditional survival ratio.
Cancel the s term.
Explain remaining lifetime under this model.

exercises.title: Choose a model carefully
exercises.prompt: Ten parts are drawn without replacement from a batch of twenty containing five defective parts. Explain why Bin(10,1/4) is not the exact defective-count model and give the exact probability expression for two defectives.
exercises.explanation: Draws are dependent. The exact hypergeometric probability is choose(5,2)*choose(15,8)/choose(20,10), counting subsets with two defectives and eight sound parts.
rubric: Identify dependence from no replacement.
Choose two of five and eight of fifteen.
Divide by the total number of ten-part subsets.

topics.name: Expectation, variance and transformations
topics.description: Compute moments and distinguish linearity from independence.

skills.name: Compute expectations
skills.description: Use weighted sums, integrals, indicators and Jensen's inequality.

skills.name: Transform variability
skills.description: Use second moments, affine scaling and covariance terms.

lesson.title: Average a function using the original law
paragraphs: For discrete X, E[g(X)]=sum g(x)p(x); for a density replace the sum by an integral. You do not need the entire distribution of g(X). Linearity E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c does not require independence. Factorizing E[XY] into E[X]E[Y] generally does.

For a fair die D, E[D]=3.5 and E[D^2]=91/6, which differs from E[D]^2. For a convex function g, Jensen's inequality gives E[g(X)]>=g(E[X]) when expectations exist. This explains the direction of the square example and warns against moving nonlinear functions outside expectations.

lesson.title: Variance tracks squared units
paragraphs: Var(X)=E[X^2]-E[X]^2 and Var(aX+b)=a^2 Var(X). For sums, Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y); independent variables have zero covariance, but zero covariance alone need not mean independence.

Worked example: E[X]=2, Var(X)=3 and Y=4-2X imply E[Y]=0 and Var(Y)=12. Shifting changes the mean but not variance; multiplication by -2 changes standard deviation by a factor of 2 and variance by 4. For indicators, E[1_A]=P(A), so expected counts can be found even when event indicators are dependent.

exercises.title: Expected score
exercises.prompt: X takes values 0,2,4 with probabilities 1/4,1/2,1/4. Find E[X].

exercises.title: Second moment
exercises.prompt: X takes values 0,2,4 with probabilities 1/4,1/2,1/4. Find Var(X).

exercises.title: Affine variance
exercises.prompt: Var(X)=3 and Y=4-2X. Find Var(Y).
exercises.explanation: The constant shift disappears and the multiplier is squared: (-2)^2*3=12.

exercises.title: Linearity with dependence
exercises.prompt: E[X]=4 and E[Y]=3, with no independence assumption. Find E[2X-Y+5].
exercises.explanation: Linearity gives 2*4-3+5=10 regardless of dependence.

exercises.title: Covariance in a sum
exercises.prompt: Var(X)=4, Var(Y)=9 and Cov(X,Y)=2. Find Var(X+Y).
exercises.explanation: 4+9+2*2=17; adding variances alone would omit dependence.

exercises.title: Jensen direction
exercises.prompt: X is positive with finite E[X] and E[1/X]. The function g(x)=1/x is convex on x>0. Which inequality follows?
exercises.explanation: Jensen for a convex g says E[g(X)]>=g(E[X]). Equality is not automatic.

exercises.title: Indicator counting
exercises.prompt: A random permutation assigns eight letters to eight envelopes, one correct envelope per letter. Let I_i indicate that letter i is correctly placed. Find the expected total number correctly placed without claiming the indicators are independent.
exercises.explanation: Each letter is correct with probability 1/8. Linearity gives sum E[I_i]=8*(1/8)=1.

exercises.title: Transform without a new density
exercises.prompt: X is uniform on [-1,2]. Compute E[X^2] directly and explain why squaring E[X] is wrong.
exercises.explanation: E[X^2]=(1/3) integral_-1^2 x^2 dx=1. E[X]=1/2, whose square is 1/4; the difference is Var(X)=3/4.
rubric: Use the uniform density 1/3 on the correct support.
Integrate x^2 to obtain 1.
Distinguish E[X^2] from (E[X])^2.

topics.name: Joint distributions and correlation
topics.description: Use support geometry, marginals and conditional densities.

skills.name: Integrate joint distributions
skills.description: Derive marginals and conditionals with support-dependent bounds.

skills.name: Interpret covariance
skills.description: Compute correlation and test independence without overclaiming.

lesson.title: Support first, integration second
paragraphs: A joint density assigns probability by integrating over a region. The marginal f_X(x)=integral f(x,y)dy must use the values of y allowed at that x. Conditional density f_Y|X(y|x)=f(x,y)/f_X(x) is defined where f_X(x)>0. Independence requires factorization over the whole support, not a single point.

For f(x,y)=2 on 0<x<y<1, integrate y from x to 1 to get f_X(x)=2(1-x). Integrating x from 0 to y gives f_Y(y)=2y. The triangular support prevents independence: knowing X close to one forces Y close to one. A constant joint density on a nonrectangular region need not yield independent coordinates.

lesson.title: Association has limits
paragraphs: Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]. Correlation divides by the two positive standard deviations and lies in [-1,1]. A constant variable has zero variance, so its correlation is undefined. Correlation measures linear association, not causation or all forms of dependence.

Worked counterexample: X uniform on [-1,1], Y=X^2. Symmetry gives E[X]=E[X^3]=0, so Cov(X,Y)=0, although knowing X determines Y. Conversely, components of a jointly Gaussian vector with zero covariance are independent; the joint Gaussian condition is essential.

exercises.title: Triangular marginal
exercises.prompt: f(x,y)=2 for 0<x<y<1, zero otherwise. What is f_X(x) for 0<x<1?
exercises.explanation: At fixed x integrate 2 over y in (x,1), giving 2(1-x).

exercises.title: Rectangle probability
exercises.prompt: (X,Y) is uniform on 0<X<4, 0<Y<2. Find P(X<Y).
exercises.explanation: The favorable area is integral_0^2 y dy=2; total area is 8, giving 1/4.

exercises.title: Conditional density
exercises.prompt: For f(x,y)=2 on 0<x<y<1, derive f_Y|X(y|x), including its support.
exercises.explanation: f_X(x)=2(1-x), so f_Y|X(y|x)=1/(1-x) for x<y<1 and 0 otherwise, for 0<x<1.
rubric: Calculate f_X(x).
Divide by the marginal.
State both the x condition and the conditional y support.

exercises.title: Covariance from moments
exercises.prompt: E[X]=2, E[Y]=3, E[XY]=8. Find Cov(X,Y).

exercises.title: Correlation scale
exercises.prompt: Cov(X,Y)=-3, Var(X)=4 and Var(Y)=9. Find the correlation.
exercises.explanation: Divide covariance by sqrt(4)*sqrt(9)=6, giving -3/6.

exercises.title: Bernoulli joint law
exercises.prompt: X,Y are Bernoulli with P(X=1)=0.6, P(Y=1)=0.5 and P(X=1,Y=1)=0.4. Find P(X=0,Y=0).
exercises.explanation: The remaining cell is 1-0.6-0.5+0.4=0.3.

exercises.title: Zero correlation counterexample
exercises.prompt: X is uniform on [-1,1] and Y=X^2. Show that X and Y are uncorrelated but dependent.
exercises.explanation: Odd moments E[X] and E[X^3] are zero, so covariance is zero. Y is a nonconstant deterministic function of X; for example |X|<1/2 forces Y<1/4.
rubric: Use symmetry for odd moments.
Compute covariance zero.
Give a concrete dependence argument.

exercises.title: Impossible covariance matrix
exercises.prompt: Can [[1,2],[2,1]] be a covariance matrix? Explain using either correlation or a linear combination's variance.
exercises.explanation: No. It would give correlation 2; alternatively Var(X-Y)=1+1-2*2=-2, which is impossible.
rubric: Identify the implied variances and covariance.
Demonstrate a violation of nonnegative variance or the correlation bound.

topics.name: Estimation, bias and mean squared error
topics.description: Evaluate estimators across repeated samples and solve moment equations.

skills.name: Construct moment estimators
skills.description: Match population moments to sample moments and check parameter support.

skills.name: Compare estimators
skills.description: Separate estimator, estimate, bias, variance and MSE.

lesson.title: A rule versus its observed value
paragraphs: An estimator is a random function T(X1,...,Xn); an estimate is the number obtained after observing the sample. Its bias for theta is E_theta[T]-theta. One observation above theta does not establish positive bias: bias describes repeated-sample behavior.

Method of moments equates theoretical moments with empirical moments. If X is uniform on [0,theta], E[X]=theta/2, giving T=2*Xbar. If two parameters are unknown, two independent moment equations are usually needed. Always check that the resulting parameter is admissible and whether it makes the observed data possible.

lesson.title: Balance bias and variability
paragraphs: MSE(T)=E[(T-theta)^2]=Var(T)+Bias(T)^2. An unbiased estimator can have larger MSE than a biased one. For iid observations with variance sigma^2, Var(Xbar)=sigma^2/n. The usual sample variance S^2=sum(Xi-Xbar)^2/(n-1) is unbiased for sigma^2; the denominator n instead estimates the normal-model MLE variance.

Worked example: estimator A has variance 4 and zero bias, so MSE 4. Estimator B has variance 1 and bias -1, so MSE 2. Under squared error B is preferable here. This comparison depends on the loss and parameter setting, not on a universal rule that bias is good or bad.

exercises.title: Moment estimate
exercises.prompt: An iid sample from Uniform(0,theta) has sample mean 6. What is the method-of-moments estimate of theta?
exercises.explanation: Match theta/2 to 6, obtaining theta_hat=12.

exercises.title: Bias correction
exercises.prompt: An estimator T satisfies E[T]=3*theta/4. Which transformation is unbiased for theta?
exercises.explanation: E[4T/3]=(4/3)(3theta/4)=theta.

exercises.title: MSE calculation
exercises.prompt: An estimator has variance 5 and bias -2. Find its MSE.
exercises.explanation: MSE=5+(-2)^2=9; the bias is squared.

exercises.title: Sample mean variance
exercises.prompt: Twenty-five iid observations each have variance 100. Find the variance of their sample mean.
exercises.explanation: Var(Xbar)=100/25=4 under independence.

exercises.title: Sample variance
exercises.prompt: For data 1,3,5, compute the unbiased sample variance using denominator n-1.
exercises.explanation: The mean is 3 and squared deviations sum to 4+0+4=8. Divide by 2.

exercises.title: One estimate does not imply bias
exercises.prompt: An unbiased estimator of a parameter equal to 10 yields 13 on today's sample. Does this contradict unbiasedness? Explain.
exercises.explanation: No. Unbiasedness means the sampling expectation is 10; individual realizations can lie above or below it.
rubric: Distinguish estimate from estimator.
Refer to repeated-sample expectation, not one error.

exercises.title: Compare squared-error risk
exercises.prompt: Estimator A has bias 0 and variance 4; B has bias 1 and variance 1. Which has lower MSE at this parameter value?
exercises.explanation: A has MSE 4; B has MSE 1+1^2=2.

exercises.title: Moment estimate support check
exercises.prompt: Assume iid Uniform(alpha,2alpha) data 10,11,19 with alpha>0. Find the moment estimate and check whether its fitted support contains every observation.
exercises.explanation: The mean is 40/3, E[X]=3alpha/2, so alpha_hat=80/9. The fitted upper endpoint is 160/9, below 19: the observed maximum is impossible under the fitted model, although population parameters from 9.5 to 10 do accommodate the data.
rubric: Calculate mean 40/3.
Compare 19 with 160/9 and identify the fitted support failure.

topics.name: Sums, generating functions and Gaussian vectors
topics.description: Derive distributions of sums and use covariance matrices correctly.

skills.name: Combine independent laws
skills.description: Use convolution and probability generating functions.

skills.name: Use multivariate normal structure
skills.description: Compute linear-combination moments and understand Gaussian independence.

lesson.title: Convolution and generating functions
paragraphs: For independent discrete X,Y, P(X+Y=s)=sum_x P(X=x)P(Y=s-x). For densities, f_(X+Y)(s)=integral f_X(x)f_Y(s-x)dx, integrating only where both factors are supported. For two independent Uniform(0,1) variables, the overlap length is s on (0,1) and 2-s on (1,2), giving a triangular density.

For a nonnegative integer-valued X, its probability generating function is G_X(z)=E[z^X]. Independence makes the pgf of a sum a product. G'_X(1)=E[X] and G''_X(1)=E[X(X-1)], so Var(X)=G''(1)+G'(1)-G'(1)^2. The second derivative is a factorial moment, not E[X^2].

lesson.title: Linear combinations of Gaussian coordinates
paragraphs: For a random vector with mean mu and covariance matrix Sigma, a^T X has mean a^T mu and variance a^T Sigma a. These moment formulas do not require Gaussianity. Joint Gaussianity additionally guarantees the linear combination is normal and that uncorrelated components are independent.
Worked example: independent X~N(1,4), Y~N(2,9) give 2X-Y~N(0,25). If instead Cov(X,Y)=1, the variance becomes 4*4+9-4=21. Writing only the diagonal terms silently assumes away covariance.

exercises.title: Convolve two indicators
exercises.prompt: Independent X~Bernoulli(1/2) and Y~Bernoulli(1/4). Find P(X+Y=1).
exercises.explanation: The disjoint cases have probabilities (1/2)(3/4) and (1/2)(1/4), totaling 1/2.

exercises.title: Triangular density
exercises.prompt: X,Y are independent Uniform(0,1). What is the density of S=X+Y at s=1/2?
exercises.explanation: For 0<s<1 the convolution integrates 1 over x in (0,s), giving f_S(s)=s.

exercises.title: Mean from a pgf
exercises.prompt: X has pgf G(z)=(0.7+0.3z)^10. Find E[X].

exercises.title: Recover variance from derivatives
exercises.prompt: A pgf satisfies G'(1)=3 and G''(1)=8. Find Var(X).

exercises.title: Gaussian combination
exercises.prompt: Independent X~N(1,4), Y~N(2,9). What is the variance of 2X-Y?
exercises.explanation: 4 Var(X)+Var(Y)=16+9=25 because the covariance term is zero.

exercises.title: Retain covariance
exercises.prompt: Var(X)=4, Var(Y)=9, Cov(X,Y)=1. Find Var(2X-Y).

exercises.title: Gaussian qualification
exercises.prompt: Two random variables each have a normal marginal distribution and zero covariance. Is that enough to conclude independence? State the stronger condition that would justify it.
exercises.explanation: Normal marginals alone do not ensure a jointly Gaussian vector. If their joint law is Gaussian, zero covariance does imply independence.
rubric: Reject the implication from marginal normality alone.
Name joint Gaussianity as the needed sufficient condition.

exercises.title: Scores through a generating function
exercises.prompt: Each of five independent rounds scores 0,1,3 with probabilities r,q,p, where p+q+r=1. Write the pgf for the total and express the probability of a total of two.
exercises.explanation: The pgf is (r+qz+pz^3)^5. Total two requires exactly two one-point rounds and three zero-point rounds: choose(5,2)q^2 r^3=10q^2 r^3.
rubric: Form the one-round pgf.
Use independence to raise it to the fifth power.
Identify the z^2 coefficient with its combinatorial factor.

topics.name: LLN, CLT and maximum likelihood
topics.description: Separate convergence from approximation and maximize likelihood with support constraints.

skills.name: Use limit theorems
skills.description: Apply Chebyshev, LLN and CLT with their assumptions and scales.

skills.name: Derive maximum-likelihood estimates
skills.description: Build likelihoods, differentiate logs and check boundaries.

lesson.title: Concentration and normal approximation
paragraphs: For finite variance, Chebyshev gives P(|X-mu|>=a)<=Var(X)/a^2. For iid averages this becomes sigma^2/(n*a^2), proving convergence in probability to mu under these assumptions. LLN says the average stabilizes; it does not say individual observations become less variable.

The iid finite-variance CLT approximates (sum Xi-n*mu)/(sigma*sqrt(n)) by N(0,1). Equivalently Xbar is approximately N(mu,sigma^2/n). For a binomial tail P(X<=k), a normal approximation commonly uses k+0.5 as continuity correction. Approximation quality depends on skewness and tail behavior, not an absolute rule that n=30 always suffices.

lesson.title: Likelihood is a function of the parameter
paragraphs: For independent observations, multiply pmfs or densities evaluated at the data, including parameter-dependent support. Take logs, find stationary points, then check boundaries and whether a maximum exists. A likelihood is not a posterior probability distribution for the parameter.

For exponential rate lambda with positive observations, log L=n log lambda-lambda sum xi, so lambda_hat=n/sum xi. For Uniform(0,theta), L=theta^-n when theta>=max xi and zero otherwise. It decreases on its admissible region, so theta_hat=max xi; differentiating without the support would miss the solution.

exercises.title: Chebyshev bound
exercises.prompt: X has mean 10 and variance 4. What is the tightest upper bound supplied by Chebyshev for P(|X-10|>=4)?
exercises.explanation: The bound is 4/4^2=1/4; Chebyshev is not generally an equality.

exercises.title: CLT for an average
exercises.prompt: An iid sample of size 100 has population mean 20 and standard deviation 10. Use the CLT and Phi(1)=0.8413 to approximate P(Xbar<=21).
exercises.explanation: The standard error is 10/sqrt(100)=1; z=(21-20)/1=1.

exercises.title: Continuity correction
exercises.prompt: X~Bin(100,1/2). When approximating P(X<=54) by a normal variable with mean 50 and standard deviation 5, which upper standardized boundary uses continuity correction?
exercises.explanation: Use (54.5-50)/5=0.9 to include the full integer cell around 54.

exercises.title: Exponential rate MLE
exercises.prompt: Four iid exponential lifetimes total two hours. What is the maximum-likelihood rate estimate in events per hour?
exercises.explanation: lambda_hat=n/sum xi=4/2=2 per hour.

exercises.title: Uniform endpoint MLE
exercises.prompt: Assume iid Uniform(0,theta) data 2,5,3 with theta>0 and endpoint support inclusive. Find the maximum-likelihood estimate of theta.
exercises.explanation: The likelihood is theta^-3 for theta>=5, zero below. It is maximized at the smallest admissible theta=5.

exercises.title: Bernoulli likelihood
exercises.prompt: An iid Bernoulli sample has seven successes and three failures. Derive the MLE of p, including how you know it is a maximum.
exercises.explanation: L=p^7(1-p)^3; the log derivative 7/p-3/(1-p)=0 gives p=0.7. The second derivative is negative in (0,1), and boundary likelihoods are zero.
rubric: Write the likelihood or log-likelihood.
Solve the derivative equation.
Check concavity or boundary behavior.

exercises.title: Limits of the CLT
exercises.prompt: A Pareto population has tail parameter alpha=1.5. Can the usual iid finite-variance CLT with sigma/sqrt(n) be justified? Explain, and distinguish the LLN.
exercises.explanation: The mean exists but variance is infinite, so that CLT and finite sigma standard error do not apply. The iid finite-mean LLN can still make the average converge to the mean.
rubric: Recognize alpha>1 gives a finite mean.
Recognize alpha<=2 gives infinite variance.
Distinguish the LLN from the stated CLT.

exercises.title: Shifted exponential support
exercises.prompt: X_i=delta+Y_i with iid Y_i~Exp(lambda), lambda>0. Data are 2,3,4. Derive the MLEs of delta and lambda, retaining the support restriction delta<=min x_i.
exercises.explanation: L=lambda^3 exp[-lambda(9-3delta)] for delta<=2. For fixed lambda it increases with delta, so delta_hat=2. Then lambda_hat=3/(9-6)=1.
rubric: Include delta<=2 in the likelihood.
Maximize at delta=2.
Optimize the remaining rate to obtain lambda=1.

topics.name: Confidence intervals and bootstrap
topics.description: Quantify estimation uncertainty and interpret coverage correctly.

skills.name: Construct confidence intervals
skills.description: Choose z, t, proportion or pivot methods and state assumptions.

skills.name: Interpret and plan uncertainty
skills.description: Explain coverage, bootstrap sampling and sample-size effects.

lesson.title: Choose the standard error and reference law
paragraphs: For iid normal data with known sigma, a two-sided mean interval is Xbar +/- z_(1-alpha/2)*sigma/sqrt(n). With unknown sigma replace sigma by S and use t_(n-1). Normality makes the latter exact; for nonnormal large samples it may be an approximation. A proportion's large-sample Wald interval is phat +/- z*sqrt(phat(1-phat)/n), but is unreliable near 0 or 1 or with sparse counts.

Worked example: n=25, Xbar=10, S=5 and supplied t_(24,0.975)=2.064 give standard error 1 and interval [7.936,12.064]. For a target half-width h with known sigma, solve n>=(z*sigma/h)^2 and round upward. Higher confidence widens the interval; quadrupling n approximately halves its width.

lesson.title: Coverage and resampling
paragraphs: In the frequentist interpretation the parameter is fixed, while the interval varies between random samples. A 95% procedure covers the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. It does not mean that 95% of individual observations fall in the interval.

For an empirical bootstrap, repeatedly sample n observations with replacement from the observed n, recompute the statistic and use the resulting distribution to estimate uncertainty. A parametric bootstrap instead simulates from a fitted model. Neither repairs selection bias or dependence automatically; ordinary iid resampling is unsuitable for strongly dependent time series. For a nonstandard pivot, first form a parameter-free probability statement, then algebraically solve it for the parameter without reversing inequalities incorrectly.

exercises.title: Known-sigma interval
exercises.prompt: An iid normal sample has n=100, mean 50 and known sigma=10. Using z=1.96, choose the 95% mean confidence interval.
exercises.explanation: The standard error is 10/10=1, so the margin is 1.96.

exercises.title: Student degrees of freedom
exercises.prompt: For a mean interval from 16 iid normal observations with unknown variance estimated by S^2, how many degrees of freedom does the t pivot have?
exercises.explanation: Estimating one mean leaves n-1=15 degrees of freedom.

exercises.title: Plan a half-width
exercises.prompt: For iid normal observations with known sigma=4, require a two-sided mean interval with half-width at most 1. Use critical value z=2. What minimum integer n is needed?
exercises.explanation: 2*4/sqrt(n)<=1 requires n>=64.

exercises.title: Proportion standard error
exercises.prompt: In 400 independent Bernoulli observations, phat=0.5. What is the estimated standard error used in the Wald interval?

exercises.title: Explain confidence
exercises.prompt: A colleague says a 95% confidence interval for the population mean contains 95% of future individual measurements. Correct this claim.
exercises.explanation: The confidence interval concerns the mean and repeated-sample coverage. Individual measurements have their own variability and require a prediction interval, generally wider.
rubric: Identify the target as a population parameter.
Explain repeated-sample coverage.
Distinguish a prediction interval for individuals.

exercises.title: Bootstrap sampling rule
exercises.prompt: You have 20 iid observations and want an ordinary empirical bootstrap estimate of the median's standard error. Describe one bootstrap replicate and how multiple replicates yield a standard error estimate.
exercises.explanation: Draw 20 observations with replacement from the original sample and compute their median. Repeat many times; the sample standard deviation of the bootstrap medians estimates standard error.
rubric: Resample the original sample size with replacement.
Recompute the median for each replicate.
Use variation between replicate medians, not raw observations.

exercises.title: Invert a maximum pivot
exercises.prompt: For iid Uniform(0,theta) observations let M be the maximum, with P(M/theta<=u)=u^n on [0,1]. Derive a one-sided 1-alpha upper confidence bound for theta using M, for 0<alpha<1.
exercises.explanation: P(M/theta>=alpha^(1/n))=1-alpha, equivalent to theta<=M/alpha^(1/n). Thus the upper bound is M/alpha^(1/n).
rubric: Choose the lower pivot cutoff alpha^(1/n).
Rearrange the inequality in the correct direction.
Give coverage 1-alpha and the upper bound.

exercises.title: Width and sample size
exercises.prompt: Under the same variance and fixed z critical value, by what integer factor must sample size increase to divide a mean interval's width by three?
exercises.explanation: Width is proportional to 1/sqrt(n); dividing it by 3 requires multiplying n by 3^2.

topics.name: Hypothesis tests, errors and power
topics.description: Design a test before observing the outcome and interpret its evidence.

skills.name: Carry out a hypothesis test
skills.description: State hypotheses, reference distribution, tail and decision.

skills.name: Interpret error probabilities
skills.description: Distinguish alpha, beta, power and p-values.

lesson.title: A reproducible testing procedure
paragraphs: Choose H0, H1 and significance level before examining the result. Compute a statistic whose distribution under H0 is known or approximated. The p-value is the null probability of a statistic at least as incompatible with H0 in the chosen direction. Reject when p<=alpha; otherwise fail to reject. A p-value is not P(H0 is true).

For iid normal data with unknown variance, T=(Xbar-mu0)/(S/sqrt(n)) has t_(n-1) under H0. For a large-sample proportion test, standardize with sqrt(p0(1-p0)/n), using the null proportion. For a normal variance test, (n-1)S^2/sigma0^2 has a chi-square distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom; the chi-square quantiles must be supplied or computed, since the archive's table sheet contains normal and t tables.

lesson.title: Errors and a worked decision
paragraphs: Type I error rejects a true null; its probability is controlled by alpha. Type II error fails to reject at a specified alternative, with probability beta; power is 1-beta. Power depends on effect size, noise, sample size and alpha. A nonsignificant result may reflect low power rather than equivalence.

Example: known sigma=4, n=16, Xbar=12, test mu0=10 versus mu>10. Z=2. If the supplied one-sided critical value is 1.645, reject at 5%. For a two-sided alternative the reference region instead compares |Z| with 1.96. Report direction, effect estimate and uncertainty alongside the decision; statistical significance does not imply practical importance.

exercises.title: One-sample statistic
exercises.prompt: An iid normal sample has n=25, mean 12 and S=5. Test H0: mu=10. What is the t statistic?

exercises.title: Two-sided normal p-value
exercises.prompt: A two-sided z test yields z=2. Given P(Z>=2)=0.0228 for standard normal Z, what is the p-value?
exercises.explanation: Symmetry gives two tails of size 0.0228, so p=0.0456.

exercises.title: Decision at a fixed level
exercises.prompt: A prespecified test has p=0.03 and alpha=0.01. What is the valid decision?
exercises.explanation: 0.03 exceeds 0.01. Failure to reject is not proof of the null.

exercises.title: Power from beta
exercises.prompt: At a specified alternative the Type II error probability is 0.2. What is the test's power there?
exercises.explanation: Power at that alternative is the probability of rejection, 1-beta=0.8.

exercises.title: Null proportion denominator
exercises.prompt: In n=100 independent Bernoulli trials, phat=0.6. For H0: p=0.5, what is the large-sample z statistic using the null standard error?
exercises.explanation: The null standard error is sqrt(0.5*0.5/100)=0.05, so z=0.1/0.05=2.

exercises.title: Variance test statistic
exercises.prompt: For n=11 iid normal observations S^2=8. Under H0: sigma^2=4, find the chi-square variance-test statistic.
exercises.explanation: (n-1)S^2/sigma0^2=10*8/4=20, with 10 null degrees of freedom.

exercises.title: Power in a normal signal model
exercises.prompt: Reject H0 when X>1.645. Under H0 X~N(0,1); at the specified alternative X~N(2,1). Express alpha and power using the standard normal cdf Phi.
exercises.explanation: Alpha=1-Phi(1.645). Power=1-Phi(1.645-2)=1-Phi(-0.355)=Phi(0.355). The two probabilities use different distributions.
rubric: Use the null law for alpha.
Standardize around mean 2 for power.
Keep the same rejection threshold.

exercises.title: Post-hoc direction
exercises.prompt: A researcher plans a two-sided mean test, then switches to a right-sided test after seeing a positive sample effect. Explain the problem and an appropriate remedy.
exercises.explanation: Choosing the direction after observing the sign changes the procedure and invalidates its nominal error control. Keep the prespecified two-sided analysis or label the finding exploratory and test the new directional hypothesis on independent data.
rubric: Identify data-dependent selection.
Explain loss of the original error guarantee.
Propose a prespecified or independent confirmatory analysis.

topics.name: Linear regression and diagnostics
topics.description: Fit and interpret simple and multiple regression, then check the model.

skills.name: Fit and interpret regression
skills.description: Compute least-squares coefficients, predictions and categorical effects.

skills.name: Assess regression assumptions
skills.description: Use residuals, R-squared, coefficient tests and transformations responsibly.

lesson.title: Least squares and coefficient meaning
paragraphs: Simple regression models Y_i=beta0+beta1*x_i+epsilon_i. Least squares minimizes RSS=sum(y_i-b0-b1*x_i)^2. When the x values vary, b1=Sxy/Sxx and b0=ybar-b1*xbar. The fitted line passes through (xbar,ybar), and with an intercept the residuals sum to zero. In multiple regression, each coefficient describes a conditional change holding the other included predictors fixed.

Worked example: (x,y)=(0,1),(1,3),(2,5) gives xbar=1, ybar=3, Sxx=2, Sxy=4, hence b1=2 and b0=1. A binary indicator D in yhat=5+2x+3D shifts the prediction by 3 relative to the D=0 reference. Use k-1 indicators for k categories when an intercept is included to avoid exact collinearity.

lesson.title: Fit is not validation
paragraphs: For least squares with an intercept, TSS=explained sum of squares+RSS and R^2=1-RSS/TSS when TSS>0. Adding predictors cannot increase training RSS, so a higher training R^2 alone does not establish a better predictive model. Residual curvature suggests a missing nonlinear term; a funnel suggests nonconstant error variance; time patterns suggest dependence.

Under independent normal errors with constant variance and a full-rank design, sigma_hat^2=RSS/(n-k-1) for k predictors and an intercept. A coefficient test uses (b_j-beta_j0)/SE(b_j) with n-k-1 degrees of freedom. Normality concerns errors, not a requirement that every predictor be normal. Log transformations change interpretation: a unit predictor increase in log(Y)=a+bx corresponds to multiplication by exp(b) on the fitted geometric scale, not addition by b to Y.

exercises.title: Fit a slope
exercises.prompt: For points (0,1),(1,3),(2,5), find the least-squares slope with an intercept.
exercises.explanation: Sxy=4 and Sxx=2, so b1=4/2=2.

exercises.title: Conditional prediction
exercises.prompt: A fitted model is yhat=5+2x+3D, where D is 0 or 1. Predict y at x=4,D=1.

exercises.title: Coefficient of determination
exercises.prompt: A least-squares fit with intercept has RSS=20 and TSS=100. Find R^2.
exercises.explanation: R^2=1-20/100=0.8. This is in-sample explained variation, not a causal claim.

exercises.title: Residual degrees of freedom
exercises.prompt: A full-rank regression fits three predictors and an intercept to 30 observations. How many residual degrees of freedom remain?
exercises.explanation: There are four fitted coefficients, leaving 30-4=26.

exercises.title: Coefficient test statistic
exercises.prompt: A regression coefficient estimate is 6 with standard error 2. For H0: beta=0, find its t statistic.
exercises.explanation: (6-0)/2=3; a decision additionally needs degrees of freedom, tail and significance level.

exercises.title: Residual funnel
exercises.prompt: Residuals remain centered near zero but their spread increases with fitted values. Which assumption is threatened, and why can the usual coefficient standard errors be misleading?
exercises.explanation: The pattern suggests heteroskedasticity. The conventional standard-error formula assumes common error variance; consider a defensible transformation or heteroskedasticity-robust inference, while investigating the mechanism.
rubric: Identify nonconstant error variance.
Connect it to the usual inference assumption.
Suggest a diagnostic or appropriate adjustment without claiming proof from the plot alone.

exercises.title: Category reference
exercises.prompt: With an intercept, how many dummy variables are needed to represent four categories without the dummy-variable trap?
exercises.explanation: Use k-1=3 indicators and a reference category. All four plus an intercept are linearly dependent.

exercises.title: Read log-scale output
exercises.prompt: A model fits log(Y)=a+0.1x+error using natural logarithms. Explain the effect of increasing x by one on the fitted exponentiated value, and why this need not equal the arithmetic conditional mean of Y.
exercises.explanation: The exponentiated fitted value is multiplied by exp(0.1), about 1.105. E[exp(error)] need not be one, so exponentiating the conditional log mean alone generally does not recover E[Y|x].
rubric: Describe the multiplicative exp(0.1) factor.
Avoid treating 0.1 as an additive change in Y.
Explain the nonlinear back-transformation issue.

topics.name: Comparisons, multiple testing and study design
topics.description: Choose paired or independent comparisons and protect error control across analyses.

skills.name: Compare populations
skills.description: Choose paired, pooled or Welch tests and interpret assumptions.

skills.name: Plan reliable inference
skills.description: Control multiplicity and connect sample size with power.

lesson.title: The sampling design chooses the test
paragraphs: Paired measurements, such as before/after on the same subjects, are analyzed through within-subject differences. A one-sample t test on those differences assumes independent normally distributed differences for exact small-sample inference. Treating the measurements as independent loses the pairing and uses the wrong variance model.

For independent normal samples with a common variance, pool S_p^2=((n1-1)S1^2+(n2-1)S2^2)/(n1+n2-2), then divide the difference of means by S_p*sqrt(1/n1+1/n2). Welch instead uses sqrt(S1^2/n1+S2^2/n2) and approximate degrees of freedom (S1^2/n1+S2^2/n2)^2 divided by ((S1^2/n1)^2/(n1-1)+(S2^2/n2)^2/(n2-1)); it does not require equal variances.

lesson.title: Multiplicity and prospective planning
paragraphs: With m independent true-null tests at level alpha, the probability of at least one rejection is 1-(1-alpha)^m. Bonferroni tests each at alpha/m and controls familywise error at most alpha without requiring independence. Specify the family of comparisons in advance; changing endpoints, subgroups or stopping rules after seeing p-values adds hidden multiplicity.

For a one-sided known-sigma normal mean test aimed at detecting a positive shift delta with power 1-beta, the planning approximation n>=[(z_(1-alpha)+z_(1-beta))*sigma/delta]^2 follows by placing the rejection threshold under the alternative distribution. Round upward and state assumed effect/noise. A larger sample detects smaller effects but does not repair biased sampling or confounding. Report the effect and uncertainty, including negative results, rather than only whether p crossed a threshold.

exercises.title: Paired measurements
exercises.prompt: The same 12 participants are measured before and after training. What observations should a paired t test analyze, and how many degrees of freedom does it use under normal independent differences?
exercises.explanation: Analyze the 12 within-person differences with a one-sample t test against zero, using 11 degrees of freedom. Independence applies between participants' differences.
rubric: Form consistent after-minus-before or before-minus-after differences.
Use a one-sample test of their mean.
State 11 degrees of freedom and independence across pairs.

exercises.title: Pooled variance
exercises.prompt: Independent normal samples have n1=n2=5, S1^2=4 and S2^2=6. Assuming equal population variances, find the pooled variance.

exercises.title: Welch standard error
exercises.prompt: Two independent samples have S1^2=9,n1=9 and S2^2=16,n2=16. What is the Welch standard error for their mean difference?
exercises.explanation: sqrt(9/9+16/16)=sqrt(2). Do not subtract variances when subtracting independent means.

exercises.title: Bonferroni threshold
exercises.prompt: You prespecify ten tests and want familywise error at most 0.05. What per-test Bonferroni significance threshold should you use?
exercises.explanation: Divide the family level by ten: 0.05/10=0.005. The union bound does not require independent tests.

exercises.title: Familywise risk
exercises.prompt: Two independent true-null tests each have exact Type I error probability 0.05. What is the probability of at least one false rejection?
exercises.explanation: The probability neither rejects is 0.95^2; its complement is 0.0975.

exercises.title: Power-based sample size
exercises.prompt: For a one-sided known-sigma normal mean test, use planning formula n>=((z_alpha+z_power)*sigma/delta)^2. Given upper-tail critical z_alpha=1.6, power quantile z_power=0.9, sigma=4 and delta=2, find the minimum integer n.
exercises.explanation: ((1.6+0.9)*4/2)^2=5^2=25. The supplied quantiles define this planning approximation.

exercises.title: Optional stopping
exercises.prompt: An analyst repeatedly adds five observations and recomputes a fixed-sample p-value, stopping at the first value below 0.05. Explain why the overall Type I error is not generally 0.05 and how to design the study responsibly.
exercises.explanation: Repeated looks create extra opportunities for rejection. Use a prespecified sample size and analysis, or a valid sequential testing design whose thresholds account for repeated monitoring; report all planned outcomes.
rubric: Recognize repeated testing over time.
Reject the claim that each look's nominal level controls the whole procedure.
Suggest fixed planning or valid sequential adjustment.

exercises.title: A nonsignificant comparison
exercises.prompt: A small study's mean-difference confidence interval is [-8,10], with a nonsignificant test against zero. Can the authors conclude the treatments are practically equivalent within +/-2? Explain.
exercises.explanation: No. The interval includes effects far outside the equivalence band. Failure to reject zero is not evidence of equivalence; a prespecified equivalence design and sufficient precision are needed.
rubric: Compare the interval with [-2,2].
Distinguish nonsignificance from equivalence.
Mention prespecified margins and adequate precision.
